'''Rosemary Fowler''' ({{née}} '''Brown'''; born 1926) is a British [[physicist]] who in 1948 as a 22-year-old doctoral researcher discovered the [[kaon]] (or K meson particle). While studying photographic plates that had been left exposed to [[cosmic ray]]s, she identified a new configuration of tracks within the photographic emulsion that she recognised as being the [[Particle decay|decay]] of an unknown charged particle. Her discovery contributed to the introduction into particle physics of the property of [[strangeness]], and to physicists' understanding that [[Parity (physics)|parity]] is not conserved in [[weak interaction]]s – features that now form an integral part of the [[Standard Model]] of particle physics.

== Early life and education ==
Born in [[Suffolk]] in 1926, Brown grew up in [[Malta]], [[Portsmouth]] and finally [[Bath, Somerset|Bath]], as her family moved to follow the postings of her father, a [[Royal Naval Engineers|Royal Naval engineer]].<ref name="Bristol">{{Cite web |date=22 July 2024 |title=Female physics pioneer, 98, honoured 75 years after discovery |url=https://www.bristol.ac.uk/news/2024/july/female-physics-pioneer-honoured.html |access-date=22 July 2024 |website=University of Bristol}}</ref> At school in wartime Bath, she excelled in maths and science, and was the only girl in her year to go to university.<ref name="Guardian">{{Cite web |last=Banfield-Nwachi |first=Mabel |date=22 July 2024 |title=Physicist, 98, honoured with doctorate 75 years after groundbreaking discovery |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/article/2024/jul/22/physicist-rosemary-fowler-honoured-doctorate-75-years-after-discovery |work=The Guardian}}</ref> In 1947, she became one of the first women to gain first class honours in physics at the [[University of Bristol]].<ref name="RAS">{{Cite web |last= |first= |title=Fowler Award (A) |url=https://ras.ac.uk/awards-and-grants/awards/2265-fowler-award-a |access-date=2024-01-16 |website=The Royal Astronomical Society |language=en}}</ref>

== Research ==
After graduating from Bristol, Brown became a doctoral researcher in the group of [[C. F. Powell|Cecil Powell]], a British physicist and pioneer in the use of [[nuclear emulsion]] coated plates to investigate cosmic rays entering the Earth's atmosphere.<ref name="Sheehy2024">{{Cite journal |last=Sheehy |first=Suzie |date=2024-01-15 |title=How a forgotten physicist's discovery broke the symmetry of the Universe |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-024-00109-5 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=625 |issue=7995 |pages=448–449 |access-date=23 July 2024 |doi=10.1038/d41586-024-00109-5|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Powell and his team had achieved success with these techniques, and had already discovered a theorised particle, the pi meson or [[pion]].<ref name="Independent">{{Cite web |last1=Massey |first1=Nina |date=22 July 2024 |title=Female physics pioneer, 98, honoured 75 years after discovery |url=https://www.msn.com/en-gb/news/uknews/physics-pioneer-98-finally-honoured-75-years-after-major-discovery/ar-BB1qnDQd |access-date=22 July 2024 |website=The Independent}}</ref>

[[File:The "k track plate" showing three-pion decay mode of a kaon, 15 Jan 1949.png|thumb|The "k track" plate showing three-pion decay of a positively-charged [[kaon]]. The kaon (''k'') enters at left and decays into a [[Pion|{{SubatomicParticle|Pion-}} meson]] (''a'') and two [[Pion|{{SubatomicParticle|Pion+}} mesons]] (''b'' and ''c''). The {{SubatomicParticle|Pion-}} meson then interacts with a [[Atomic nucleus|nucleus]] in the [[Nuclear emulsion|emulsion]] at ''B''.]]

Working alongside her fellow PhD student and future husband [[Peter Fowler (physicist)|Peter Fowler]], Brown studied the tracks left on stacks of photographic plates that were exposed to cosmic rays at the [[Sphinx Observatory]], a high-altitude laboratory at [[Jungfraujoch]], [[Switzerland]]. When Minnie van der Merwe, one of the team of "scanners" (non-physicist assistants), passed her a plate with an unusual configuration of tracks, Brown recognised it as a candidate for the [[Particle decay|decay]] of a new [[meson]], called at that time the 'tau meson' (not to be confused with the entirely different [[elementary particle]] currently called the [[Tau (particle)|tau]]).<ref name="Sheehy2024" /> The group published their findings in a 1949 paper in [[Nature (journal)|''Nature'']]<ref name="Nature">{{Cite journal |last=Brown |first=R |author-link=Rosemary Fowler |last2=Camerini |first2=U |last3=Fowler |first3=PH |author-link3=Peter Fowler (physicist) |last4=Muirhead |first4=H |last5=Powell |first5=CF |author-link5=C. F. Powell |last6=Ritson |first6=DM |date=15 January 1949 |title=Observations with Electron-Sensitive Plates Exposed to Cosmic Radiation. Part 2. Further Evidence for the Existence of Unstable Charged Particles, of Mass ∼ 1,000 me, and Observations on their Mode of Decay |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=163 |pages=82–87 |doi=10.1038/163082a0}}</ref> which included a photograph of what became known as the 'k track' plate.

Brown's 'tau meson' appeared similar to the 'theta meson' that had been discovered earlier by [[George Rochester|G.D. Rochester]] and [[Clifford Butler|C.C. Butler]] of the University of Manchester,<ref name="Strange">{{Cite journal|last1=Yamanaka|first1=Taku|title=Detection of a strange particle|journal=Nature|URL=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-019-02841-9|volume=575|pages=36–38|date=4 Nov 2019|access-date=23 July 2024|doi=10.1038/d41586-019-02841-9}}</ref> except that it decayed into three pions rather than the two of the 'theta meson'.<ref name="Sheehy2024" /> Since the two decay paths have different [[Parity (physics)|parities]], the physics of the time suggested that in spite of their apparent similarity the particles could not be the same (the 'theta-tau puzzle'). The puzzle was later resolved by the introduction into the theory of a new [[strangeness]] quantum number, and by the 1957 experimental discovery that parity was not conserved by the [[weak interaction]] (the fundamental interaction that governs kaon decay).<ref name="Strange" />

Powell was awarded the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1950 "for his development of the photographic method of studying nuclear processes and his discoveries regarding mesons made with this method."<ref name="Nobel">{{Cite web |title=The Nobel Prize in Physics 1950 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1950/summary/ |access-date=23 July 2024 |website=The Nobel Prize}} More details: A.E. Lindh (1950) "[https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1950/ceremony-speech/ Nobel Presentation Speech]" (retrieved 23 July 2024).</ref>

== Personal life and legacy==
Rosemary Brown and [[Peter Fowler (physicist)|Peter Fowler]] married in 1949.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wolfendale |first=Arnold |date=January 1998 |title=Peter Howard Fowler. 27 February 1923–8 November 1996 |url=https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rsbm.1998.0012 |journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |language=en |volume=44 |pages=177–189 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.1998.0012  |doi-access=free|issn=0080-4606|url-access=subscription }}</ref> She never completed her doctorate, but continued to assist her husband while  raising their three daughters<ref name="Sheehy2024" /> – one of whom, the geophysicist [[Mary Fowler (geologist)|Mary Fowler]], became [[Master (college)|Master]] of [[Darwin College, Cambridge]].

In 2004, Rosemary Fowler supported the [[Royal Astronomical Society]] to establish the Fowler award for early achievement in astronomy, in memory of her husband Peter and her father-in-law [[Ralph H. Fowler]].<ref name="RAS" />

== Awards ==
In July 2024, at the age of 98, Fowler was awarded an [[Honorary degree|honorary doctorate]] of science by the [[University of Bristol]].<ref name="Bristol" /><ref name="Guardian" /> The university stated "Rosemary's discovery of particles and contribution to our understanding of fundamental interactions in physics has often been attributed to Powell and her husband Peter Fowler, and this honorary degree acknowledges the vital role she has played in science."<ref name="UofB">{{Cite web |title=Rosemary Fowler : Doctor of Science |url=https://www.bristol.ac.uk/graduation/ceremonial-guide/rosemary-fowler/ |access-date=15 July 2024 |website=University of Bristol}}</ref> Presenting the award, [[Paul Nurse|Sir Paul Nurse]], Chancellor of the University of Bristol, said "Rosemary's work in particle discovery in the 1940s, as a physicist at Bristol, paved the way for critical discoveries that continue to shape the work of today's physicists, and our understanding of the universe."<ref name="Darwin">{{Cite web |date=17 July 2024 |access-date=22 July 2024 |title=University of Bristol recognises contribution to physics of Rosemary Fowler |url=https://www.darwin.cam.ac.uk/news/university-of-bristol-recognises-contribution-to-physics-of-rosemary-fowler/ |website=Darwin College, Cambridge}}</ref> Dr Fowler said that she felt "very honoured" and that she had not "done any thing since to deserve special respect."<ref name="Independent" />
